clinicalPearls: X-linked hypophosphataemia is the commonest heritable form of rickets and osteomalacia, inherited as an X-linked dominant trait caused by loss-of-function mutations in PHEX.
Loss of PHEX function leads to excess circulating FGF23, which drives renal phosphate wasting and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylation, giving an inappropriately normal or low calcitriol.

Biochemistry shows low phosphate with high urinary phosphate (low TmP/GFR), normal calcium, normal or low 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D, normal or mildly raised PTH, raised alkaline phosphatase and raised or inappropriately normal FGF23.
Unlike nutritional rickets, calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are normal and there is no hypocalcaemia or tetany.
Children present with leg bowing, short stature, a waddling gait, delayed walking and spontaneous dental abscesses.

Conventional treatment with oral phosphate salts plus active vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) risks nephrocalcinosis and secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism, and requires careful monitoring.
The anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody burosumab is now preferred for children and selected adults, improving phosphate handling and healing rickets.
Adults may have persistent osteomalacia, pseudofractures, enthesopathy, degenerative arthritis, dental sepsis and, from childhood, craniosynostosis.
reference.pathophysiology: PHEX encodes an endopeptidase expressed in osteoblasts and osteocytes. Its loss of function leads, through incompletely defined signalling, to overproduction of the phosphaturic hormone FGF23 by bone cells. Elevated FGF23 acts on the proximal renal tubule to downregulate the sodium-phosphate cotransporters NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc, causing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia. FGF23 simultaneously suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase and stimulates 24-hydroxylase, so calcitriol is inappropriately low or normal rather than rising in response to hypophosphataemia. Chronic hypophosphataemia impairs mineralisation of the growth plate (rickets) and of osteoid in mature bone (osteomalacia).
additionalDifferentials: autosomal dominant or recessive hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1)
hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH, SLC34A3)
additionalInvestigations: serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and PTH
wrist and knee radiographs and DXA
redFlags: nephrocalcinosis or declining renal function on conventional treatment
tertiary hyperparathyroidism developing during phosphate therapy
spinal canal stenosis or cord compression from enthesopathy and ligament ossification
reference.prognosis: This is a lifelong condition; with treatment growth and deformity improve, but many adults have residual short stature, enthesopathy, degenerative joint disease and dental problems.
pitfalls: misdiagnosing as nutritional rickets and giving only nutritional vitamin D, which is ineffective
failing to monitor for treatment-induced nephrocalcinosis
over-treatment provoking secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism
references: Oxford Textbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
management: Conventional therapy with oral phosphate salts combined with an active vitamin D analogue such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol to promote mineralisation
Consideration of the anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody burosumab in eligible patients as targeted disease-directed therapy
Regular biochemical monitoring of phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, calcium and parathyroid hormone during treatment
Renal ultrasound surveillance for nephrocalcinosis and vigilance for secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Orthopaedic assessment and corrective surgery for persistent lower-limb deformity
Dental surveillance and prompt treatment of spontaneous dental abscesses
Multidisciplinary metabolic bone follow-up spanning paediatric-to-adult transition
Genetic counselling for the X-linked dominant trait and screening of at-risk relatives
